structure.overview: The case concerns the Applicant's motion for mandamus relief to compel the Respondent to decide on a permanent residence application within a set timeframe. The Applicant challenges delays in the security screening process and seeks expedited judicial review, while the Respondent opposes the motion. The Federal Court dismissed the motion, finding no exceptional circumstances to justify mandamus and rejecting the Applicant's supplemental evidence and arguments for expedited relief.

party_points.text: Completed medical exam, biometrics, responded to requests
Filed for leave and judicial review seeking mandamus to compel PR decision within 30 days
New evidence updates factual matrix; no prejudice to Respondent
Over three years delay causes harm; Court should expedite leave application
Claims exceptional circumstances and new evidence shows exceptionality; denies bypassing leave or queue jumping
Rule 8(1) does not apply as no timelines fixed for leave decision
Section 72(1) IRPA bars judicial review without leave; jurisdictional bar
New evidence won't affect Court's decision on justification for delay

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Respondent opposes the motion; parties await decision on leave for judicial review where Applicant seeks mandamus to compel PR decision.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court dismisses the motion for the reasons that follow.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant completed medical exam, biometrics, and responded to further information requests in the application process.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: IRCC reviewed the Applicant’s application and initiated a security review.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: On February 17, 2025, the Applicant filed for leave and judicial review seeking mandamus to compel decision on PR application within 30 days or set time.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: On April 23, 2025, the Respondent filed its memorandum of argument and affidavit.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: On April 25, 2025, the Applicant filed his reply memorandum of argument.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: No Immigration Rules provisions allow filing evidence on Reply; supplemental evidence requires special circumstances under Rule 55 and Ahmed at para 13.

citations.cite: Federal Courts Citizenship, Immigration and Refugee Protection Rules, SOR/93-22
citations.why: States no evidence filing on Reply except special circumstances under Rule 55

citations.cite: Ahmed v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2025 FC 929 at para 13
citations.why: Defines special circumstances test for filing supplemental evidence

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court follows Ahmed's factors to determine special circumstances for supplemental evidence: availability, relevance, and prejudice.

citations.cite: Ahmed v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2025 FC 929 at para 15
citations.why: Lists factors for granting leave to file supplemental evidence

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant failed to prove special or unusual circumstances to file supplementary reply evidence.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Respondent concedes evidence availability but court agrees Applicant fails other two test elements for supplemental evidence.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicant argues new evidence updates factual matrix and Respondent is not prejudiced by it.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Respondent shows new evidence does not complete security review; Applicant acknowledges CSIS screen is only one step.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Applicant fails second test element as evidence won't affect Court's decision on Respondent's justification for delay.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Admitting new evidence prejudices Respondent by depriving response opportunity; Respondent filed evidence on screening steps not before leave judge.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Filing supplemental reply evidence conflicts with Immigration Rules' philosophy to ensure expeditious leave applications; supported by Taiyese and Ahmed.
idea_list: Supplemental evidence conflicts with Rules' philosophy
Cites Taiyese and Ahmed supporting expeditious process

citations.cite: Taiyese v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2024 FC 1730 at paras 19-20
citations.why: Supports expeditious processing under Immigration Rules

citations.cite: Ahmed v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2025 FC 929 at para 22
citations.why: Supports expeditious processing under Immigration Rules

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Applicant attempts to split case by new affidavit after Minister's response, giving inappropriate advantage.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicant argues over three years delay causes harm and Court should expedite leave application without unfairness to others.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Respondent argues Rule 8(1) does not apply as no timelines fixed by Rules or Court Order for leave decision.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Justice Diner in Ezimokhai says timeline for leave decision is Court's prerogative and exclusive jurisdiction.

citations.cite: Ezimokhai v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1452 at para 11
citations.why: Court controls timeline for leave decision

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court agrees Rule 8(1) cannot compel leave decision; same fundamental impediment applies as in Ezimokhai.

citations.cite: Ezimokhai v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1452 at para 12

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Associate Justice Horne notes many litigants seek priority; granting relief would prioritize Applicant over others.

citations.cite: Lu v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) IMM-3585-25, June 25, 2025, para 9
citations.why: Notes many litigants seek priority in immigration matters

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Section 72(1) IRPA bars judicial review without leave; cited Farhadi and Varela supporting this jurisdictional bar.
idea_list: Section 72(1) IRPA bars judicial review without leave
Cites Farhadi and Varela supporting bar

citations.cite: Section 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27
citations.why: States Court's jurisdiction and leave requirement

citations.cite: Farhadi v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) 2014 FC 926 at para 18
citations.why: Supports leave requirement for judicial review

citations.cite: Varela v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) 2009 FCA 145 at para 24
citations.why: Supports leave requirement for judicial review

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicant claims exceptional circumstances and new evidence shows exceptionality; denies bypassing leave or queue jumping.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court rejects Applicant's claim of exceptional circumstances justifying extraordinary remedy.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court agrees mandamus relief is like summary judgment, which is unavailable under Immigration Rules; citing Lu para 11.

citations.cite: Lu v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) IMM-3585-25, June 25, 2025, para 11
citations.why: Mandamus akin to summary judgment not available under Immigration Rules

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court acknowledges Applicant's frustration but stresses importance of security screening for immigration system integrity and public confidence.
